subtopic: A conflict between two team members
subtype: Approach: root cause analysis with five whys [Thinking]
passage: I'm Samir, and I was in the room when Simran sat down with Anil and Tanya after their third argument that month. Simran did not ask who was to blame. "Why did the deploy fail?" "Because the config was old." "Why was it old?" "Because I thought Tanya updated it," Anil said. "Why did you think that?" "Because we both had that ticket." "And why did you both have it?" Silence. Then Anil said, "Nobody wrote down who owns it." Simran wrote two lines on the whiteboard: overlap, and no handover note. The tension in the room dropped. I can't say if Simran planned to ask so many times. It just kept going until it stopped being about personalities.

qa.q: What two things did Simran write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Simran wrote overlap, and no handover note.

qa.q: What might Anil have been feeling when saying nobody wrote down who owns it?
qa.a: Anil probably felt a mix of relief and some embarrassment at seeing that the problem was not personal.

qa.q: What else could Simran do once the cause was found, and why?
qa.a: Simran could set a single owner per ticket and a handover note, because that removes the overlap that kept creating blame.

qa.q: How might Tanya have felt when the questions stayed off blame?
qa.a: Tanya probably felt relieved and less defensive, seeing that the trouble came from how the work was assigned.

grounding: Illustrates a lead asking why repeatedly and finding overlapping assignments and a missing handover note behind the quarrel, not personalities.

subtopic: A conflict between two team members
subtype: Approach: root cause analysis with five whys [Thinking]
passage:
Monday. Karthik and Neelam had snapped at each other again in the sprint review. Harsha, their lead, wrote the question on a sticky note: why do they keep fighting? Her first answer was "they just don't get along," but she crossed it out. Why did today's fight start? Because Karthik's test cases failed on Neelam's code.
Wednesday. Harsha kept going. Why did they fail? Neelam changed the login flow. Why didn't Karthik know? There was no handover note. Why no note? Because the task was assigned to both of them, and each thought the other would write it. "It's not personality," she muttered. "It's the board."
The next Monday. Harsha split the overlapping tasks so each had one owner and added a handover box to every card. By Friday, the review passed without a single sharp remark.

qa.q: What did Harsha add to every card?
qa.a: She added a handover box to every card.

qa.q: How did Harsha's thinking change when she crossed out "they just don't get along"?
qa.a: She moved from a frustrated guess about personalities to curious questioning, and she felt clearer once she saw the overlapping assignments were creating the blame.

qa.q: What else could Harsha try if the fighting had continued after the change?
qa.a: She could meet each of them separately to hear what they need, in case there is a second cause the whys did not reach.

qa.q: How might Karthik experience the change on the board?
qa.a: Karthik no longer gets surprised by code changes nobody mentioned, so Karthik may feel less blamed and less defensive in reviews.

grounding: It shows a lead asking why repeatedly and finding that overlapping task assignments and a missing handover note, not personality, keep causing blame.

subtopic: A conflict between two team members
subtype: Approach: root cause analysis with five whys [Thinking]
passage:
Naveen, you look like you want to quit this team. Sit. Let me tell you about the year I, Vishal, first became a shift lead at the textile mill.
I had two supervisors, Lakshman and Pereira, who fought every week. I thought, these two men simply cannot stand each other. My own boss told me, don't look at the men, look at the reasons. Ask why five times.
So I asked. Why the fight? A dye batch came out wrong. Why? Pereira used the old recipe. Why? Nobody told him Lakshman had changed it. Why not? There was no handover book between shifts. Why? Because both of them were listed in charge of the dye room, so each thought the other wrote it down.
It was never their tempers, Naveen. It was my duty chart. I gave the dye room one owner and started a handover book.
Try the whys before you try to leave.

qa.q: What came out wrong at the textile mill?
qa.a: A dye batch came out wrong.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel about the two supervisors before asking why?
qa.a: Vishal felt frustrated and was sure the two men simply could not stand each other.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vishal's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: The turning point was the boss telling Vishal to look at the reasons, not the men; that pushed Vishal to ask why five times and find the duty chart problem he could fix.

qa.q: How might Pereira have felt once the dye room had one owner?
qa.a: Pereira would probably feel relieved and less blamed, because he would know who changed recipes and could read the handover book instead of guessing.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how asking why repeatedly revealed that overlapping duties and a missing handover record, not personality, kept two supervisors quarrelling.
